item.title: Why Pakistan needs administrative restructuring. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan’s administrative map is carrying a population load it was never designed for. We are now a country of more than 240 million people.

Punjab alone is home to over 127 million people, Sindh more than 55 million and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa over 40 million. These numbers matter beyond being a headcount from a census. They help decide how far the government has to reach, how many people local institutions must serve, how development funds are shared and how fast the state can act.

Yet the spaces where political power, financial decisions and government action are concentrated remain very few. At the national level, Pakistan has only 266 directly elected National Assembly seats for a population of 241.5 million, averaging roughly one directly elected representative for every 908,000 people.

Overtly concentrated

Government is heavily concentrated in Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar and Quetta. Ministries, senior bureaucracies, large hospitals, universities, courts and development authorities gather around provincial capitals. Over time, economic activity follows them, as do jobs, professional services, infrastructure and investment. Such concentration has consequences for regions farther away.

A citizen in southern Punjab experiences provincial government differently from someone in Lahore. The same holds for Hazara in relation to Peshawar, or for distant districts in Sindh and Balochistan. Geography eventually becomes administrative distance. Files move through longer chains, senior decision-makers remain elsewhere and development priorities compete for attention with those of much larger metropolitan centres. This is exactly why the debate over new administrative units deserves to be linked directly with prosperity.

In economics, government exerts a gravitational pull. A centre of administration creates surrounding departments, courts, universities, hospitals, infrastructure, housing, services and jobs, and this draws businesses towards it. It also fosters professional communities; roads are built or improved, land prices rise and new markets form. All these dynamics can be seen across Pakistan around existing provincial capitals. There is, therefore, no real reason to assume that the same institutional pull would not help build additional regional growth centres.

South Punjab is an obvious example of this administrative logic. The establishment of the South Punjab Secretariat in 2020 acknowledged the problem caused by placing all authority in Lahore. One of its stated purposes was to allow people in the area to have their issues resolved closer to where they live. This recognition was important because it accepted that proximity to government has both economic and social value.

Similarly, Hazara has demanded a separate province for many years. In August 2026, proponents again linked the demand with demographic growth, governance and administrative feasibility. Previously, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Assembly had adopted resolutions in favour of a separate province of Hazara. Bahawalpur has a similar history of demand for a separate province, and that demand persists. A rally calling for the restoration of the province of Bahawalpur was held in August 2026.

New centres of gravity

Although each of these regions has its own history and political environment, what unites them is the desire for better access to the state’s institutions, greater representation and a greater share of development. Giving these areas their own “economic centre of gravity” would involve creating a new provincial capital with all its attendant institutions: universities would expand and hospitals would gain specialised departments, among other things, providing professional employment opportunities.

As the private sector responds to public investment and the movement of people, a region that relies heavily on a distant provincial capital for the income generated by administrative activity will, over time, begin to develop its own administrative and commercial ecosystems. This is when the issue of prosperity becomes most relevant.

Balanced development is also difficult to achieve where opportunity is spatially concentrated. Young people should not have to migrate to Lahore, Karachi or other large cities for opportunities such as quality education, decent jobs and access to specialist services. Establishing other centres of administration could help spread some of these opportunities.

There is also a simple administrative benefit. Governments can gain a more thorough overview of the people within smaller jurisdictions, attend to needs specific to the district and monitor the progress of schools, hospitals, roads and other such projects. Regional budgets can better reflect such differences in conditions.

Lessons from overseas

Regional experience offers similar examples. India created Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand in 2000 to give greater administrative and development focus to distinct regions, while Bangladesh later created Mymensingh as a separate administrative division.

Another example is Indonesia, which in 2022 created new provinces in Papua, stating that the goals were to shorten administrative reach, improve public services, make development more focused and reduce regional disparities. President Joko Widodo called the division an attempt to make development more equitable across a territory too large to be managed in this way. The comparison is relevant to Pakistan because of its own combination of population growth, geographical distance and differential development.

Local government is especially important. Prosperity spreads more effectively when authority reaches municipalities and districts rather than remaining concentrated at the provincial tier. Provincial restructuring can create the larger framework, while stronger local institutions carry that change into towns and communities.

The process also has to reflect public aspiration. Credible surveys, consultations and economic feasibility work can help establish where demand is strongest and what form people expect restructuring to take. The Constitution already provides a demanding route: Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment to receive two-thirds support in both Houses of Parliament, while an amendment altering a province’s limits also requires two-thirds approval of the affected provincial assembly. That framework gives administrative restructuring the scale of national reform it deserves.

Pakistan’s population will continue to grow. Its secondary cities will expand, regional economies will become more important and pressure on existing provincial centres will increase. Governance structures eventually have to respond to that reality. A more distributed administrative system offers a route towards a more distributed economy as well. More centres of government can mean more centres of education, healthcare, employment, investment and political representation.

For a country seeking broader prosperity, that is a possibility worth examining seriously.

item.title: Finding solutions to cost of living. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is unfortunate to see recent figures which showcase that tax relief has resulted in no real reduction in the unusually high or fluctuating market prices -- a clear disservice to consumers who deserve some financial relief on basic goods.
The government reduced duties and taxes on 63 essential commodities in the FY27 budget, including rice, pulses, edible oil, spices, and agricultural products. Yet prices of many of these goods have remained high or even increased.
Reducing taxes and duties on essential goods is a welcome step when the cost of living continues to put pressure on ordinary families. However, this glaring gap between policy and reality remains a serious concern.
There are legitimate factors behind some of these increases: Traders have pointed to higher fuel costs, energy shortages, floods, heavy rainfall, and disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
While these pressures cannot simply be dismissed, they should not become a blanket explanation for every price increase either.
The onus is, therefore, on the government to strengthen market monitoring and determine where the benefits of tax concessions are going. If importers, wholesalers, or intermediaries are absorbing the savings instead of passing them on, consumers are effectively being denied the relief that public policy intended to provide.
This is particularly important at this point in time, when household budgets are already stretched; recent reporting has found families cutting back on food and household necessities as everyday expenses continue to rise.
Tax reductions should be accompanied by transparency, competition, and effective oversight. Relevant agencies need to regularly compare import costs, wholesale prices, and retail prices, and take action where unjustified margins or manipulation are found.
The objective of tax relief should ultimately be clear: Making essential goods more affordable.
The government has taken the first step, but now it must ensure that the benefit actually reaches the people it was meant to help.

item.title: Saving Dhaka’s lakes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to strengthen coordinated efforts to prevent pollution and improve the environment of the lakes in Gulshan, Banani, Baridhara, Niketan, and Dhanmondi must be taken seriously and heeded.
For too long, these lakes, which ought to -- beyond being vital urban ecosystems that regulate drainage and reduce flooding -- provide respite and peace to the citizens of Dhaka, have instead been reduced to polluted messes as a result of years of sewage discharge, illegal connections, sludge buildup, and institutional neglect.
If Dhaka fails to act now with discipline and coordination, these fast-deteriorating water bodies will slip beyond recovery.
Of course, we are well aware that the pollution is not accidental. Sewage enters Gulshan Lake through at least a dozen identified points while buildings bypass proper sewerage systems and dump waste directly into stormwater drains. This is mismanagement and a lack of regard of the highest order, and needs immediate correction.
Beyond the coordination, and for Wasa and the city corporations to work together, we need people within the administration who recognize the magnitude of the issue and actually care to find solutions. There is simply no justification for the city’s lakes to be in such a polluted state, and that year after year, decade after decade, it has only gotten worse is embarrassing.
The deployment of special teams is encouraging, but teams alone cannot fix a system that has allowed pollution to flourish for decades. Dhaka needs accountability, with real consequences for offenders as well as those responsible for action but failing to do so.
As among the least liveable cities in the world, these water bodies must become clean, functional, and protected to offer some respite to an increasingly frustrated citizenry. With the PM himself recognizing the importance, there can be no more excuses.

item.title: A legacy written at the UN. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
At the United Nations General Assembly later this month, when Prime Minister Tarique Rahman speaks, he will enter a domain in which his parents have already spoken on behalf of what Bangladesh needed from the world.
This will add yet another page to a long political history that dates back almost half a century.
In 1980, President Ziaur Rahman addressed the United Nations at a special session which was dominated by the oil crisis and the growing economic gap between developed and developing countries. Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, meanwhile, first addressed the General Assembly in 1991, after the BNP’s election victory brought her to office as PM, and returned to the UN podium in 2005 during her third term.
Now Tarique Rahman is poised to make his speech during the 81st session of the General Assembly when Bangladesh will take the chairmanship.
It was different every time. The international system was different as well. There is, however, one thing in common: The need for Bangladesh to exercise its agency to define and pursue its national interest.
Ziaur Rahman expressed it in the language of 1980.
The oil shock had exposed how vulnerable poorer countries were to decisions made elsewhere. In his UN address, he questioned the imbalance between huge global military expenditure and declining development assistance. He linked international peace with the economic divide between rich and poor countries and called for changes to the global trade, financial, and development system.
For Bangladesh, he placed agriculture, rural development, and food production high on the national agenda. At the same time, he pressed developed countries for better market access, more development assistance, and debt relief.
His address was summed up in one phrase: “Self-reliance.” It was not a call for isolation. Ziaur Rahman was arguing for a Bangladesh that could rely more on its own productive capacity while working with other countries to secure a fairer international order.
Khaleda Zia’s first UN address came in a very different Bangladesh. The country had just returned to parliamentary democracy. The available material from her 1991 speech points to concerns that were immediate and national: Democratic governance, the sharing of common river waters, recovery from the April cyclone, rural development and poverty reduction, and greater attention to women’s education and maternal and child health.
The subjects were largely domestic. The forum was global. That was part of the point. Bangladesh was taking its own problems to an international audience, rather than allowing the country to be defined solely by the crises it faced.
By 2005, Khaleda Zia was speaking from a different position again. Her address covered UN reform, terrorism, human rights, development, the interests of least developed countries, and peacekeeping. Bangladesh was still making demands of the international system, but it was also presenting itself as a country with responsibilities within that system.
She pointed to Bangladesh’s contribution to UN peacekeeping and its role in international efforts on peace and security. The message was broader than development assistance: Bangladesh had interests to defend, but it also had something to contribute.
That thread helps put Tarique Rahman’s “Bangladesh First” policy in perspective. The phrase is new. The underlying instinct is older.
Ziaur Rahman spoke of self-reliance. Khaleda Zia placed democracy, development, sovereignty, and Bangladesh’s international responsibilities at the centre of her UN interventions. Tarique Rahman is now putting national interest more explicitly at the heart of his foreign-policy language.
There are parallels elsewhere. India’s Nehru-Gandhi family produced three generations of prime ministers. Sri Lanka’s Bandaranaike family saw political power pass across generations as well. But political inheritance does not come with a script. Every generation meets a different world.
That is where Tarique Rahman’s UN appearance becomes more than a family milestone. The world in which he will speak has almost nothing in common with the world in which Ziaur Rahman operated in 1980. Bangladesh is not the young nation overly dependent on foreign aid that it was then. Its economy, diplomatic interests, and international role have changed. So have the questions confronting it, from climate change and economic security to shifting geopolitical alliances and the Rohingya crisis.
The old question of national agency remains, but its meaning has become more complicated. A country cannot put its interests first simply by looking inward. The interests of Bangladesh are such that they are related to what goes on outside the country. Protecting national interests has become more about managing competing influences.
That is the test of any political legacy. Ziaur Rahman used the UN to argue for greater economic self-reliance and a stronger voice for developing countries. Khaleda Zia used it to speak about Bangladesh’s democratic transition, development concerns and responsibilities in international affairs. Tarique Rahman now has the opportunity to give his own meaning to “Bangladesh First.”
His speech will inevitably be compared with those of his parents. But the more useful comparison may be with the country itself. Bangladesh will be presiding over the General Assembly as Tarique Rahman speaks. The country that once went to the UN asking for greater room to develop is now in a position to shape part of the institution’s agenda.
That is perhaps the clearest measure of how much has changed since 1980. The family’s UN history, in that sense, is also a condensed history of Bangladesh’s changing place in the world. The central idea has survived, but the circumstances have not.
Jobair Babu is a filmmaker, columnist, and broadcaster.

item.title: Reimagining the ‘human’ in HR. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Artificial intelligence is no longer a distant vanguard discussed exclusively at Silicon Valley tech symposiums. It has fundamentally begun to reshape the topography of recruitment and workforce management in Bangladesh in concrete, measurable terms.
Consider a scenario numbers-driven HR professionals know all too well: A single entry-level vacancy in Dhaka can easily attract several thousand digital submissions. Where manual screening once demanded days of cognitive exhaustion and carried a profound risk of overlooking non-traditional yet highly qualified talent, AI-powered applicant tracking systems (ATS) and parsing algorithms can now sift through the deluge within minutes.
This transformation is unfolding across a diverse spectrum of the Bangladeshi economy stretching from multinational conglomerates and forward-thinking financial institutions to local enterprises and business process outsourcing (BPO) firms.
However, at present, employees harbour deep-seated anxieties regarding job security, middle management questions the long-term relevance of traditional supervisory roles, and organizations struggle to demarcate where human capability ends and machine intelligence begins.
This concern is far from unfounded. The pertinent question confronting us today is whether our institutional capacity for human adaptation can keep pace with technological acceleration equitably.
Human resources in Bangladesh must therefore transcend its legacy role of administrative processing and consciously assume a more visionary mandate: Becoming the deliberate architect of human potential in an AI-driven economy.
The most immediate demonstration of AI adoption in Bangladeshi HR is undisputed operational liberation. Automated resume screening, biometric, and AI-driven attendance metrics, algorithmic payroll configuration, and AI chatbots managing preliminary candidate communication have radically optimized workflows.
Yet, this efficiency does not exist in a vacuum; it arrives with a distinct societal cost.
A definitive study conducted by the Bangladesh Labour Foundation (BLF) in collaboration with researchers from BRAC University surveyed garment workers across the industrial hubs of Dhaka, Gazipur, and Narayanganj. The findings were sobering: Technological automation had already contracted overall employment in specific RMG segments by nearly one-third, with sweater production and woven-garment assembly lines bearing the brunt of the transition.
Crucially, those displaced were disproportionately helpers, older workers, and women with limited formal education -- the exact demographic possessing the fewest alternative economic prospects.
The socio-economic impact of this shift depends entirely on where a worker stands in the economy. The scope of automation varies drastically between sectors. In the manufacturing and RMG sectors, AI threatens to replace entire physical roles and eliminate low-skill positions, placing vulnerable labor at severe risk.
Conversely, in knowledge-intensive corporate environments, AI functions differently. It primarily automates discrete tasks rather than whole professions, augmenting human analytical power and reallocating valuable time toward strategic thinking
This is the stark reality that hyper-optimistic tech narratives often gloss over. In labour-intensive manufacturing, automation does not merely absorb tedious sub-tasks; it threatens to eliminate entire categories of entry-level employment.
Advanced computerized knitting machines and automated fabric cutters are shifting the industry standard. The ethical imperative for modern HR leadership is to mitigate this displacement deliberately through structured corporate retraining frameworks, upskilling initiatives, and equitable severance packages ensuring a "just transition" rather than a chaotic fallout.
Conversely, in knowledge-intensive corporate landscapes -- such as tech startups like Pathao and Chaldal, or pioneering mobile financial services (MFS) giants like bKash - the dynamic is entirely different. In these environments, AI acts as an augmentative tool rather than a replacement, automating repetitive tasks rather than whole professions.
When HR professionals in these settings are unburdened from the tyranny of bureaucratic paperwork, they gain the strategic bandwidth required to focus on macro workforce planning, employee mental well-being, and organizational culture. Bangladesh's AI narrative is not monolithic; it is a tale of two distinct workforces, contingent entirely upon a worker's position within the economic hierarchy.
The structural mismatch and the algorithmic bias
The most formidable structural bottleneck to our digital evolution remains the systemic mismatch between tertiary academic output and contemporary industry demands.
While progressive employers increasingly look for sophisticated digital literacy, data fluency, and adaptive analytical capabilities, conventional academic curricula often remain stuck in a legacy system that rewards memorization over applied reasoning. The modern corporate ecosystem no longer requires graduates to compete against machine intelligence; it requires professionals who can creatively collaborate with it.
Government initiatives have begun laying the groundwork to bridge this gap. The state has articulated ambitious targets to catalyze the ICT sector’s contribution to national GDP. However, the execution of most initiatives faces a critical challenge: The stark urban-rural digital divide. The infrastructure heavily favours metropolitan centres like Dhaka and Chittagong.
Furthermore, a less apparent but equally hazardous risk lies in the deployment of AI-driven recruitment engines. If an AI screening tool is trained on historical corporate data, it risks inadvertently encoding past biases -- such as disproportionately favouring resumes that feature elite, urban universities or specific affluent postal codes.
Without rigorous algorithmic auditing and conscious oversight by HR departments, these automated systems may institutionalize a digital glass ceiling, systematically excluding brilliant talent originating from rural or underprivileged backgrounds.
As machine learning systematically absorbs the administrative overhead of corporate operations, HR departments are uniquely positioned to reclaim their true purpose. The efficacy of a modern HR department should no longer be audited merely through the lens of cost reduction, but through the metrics of workforce resilience and sustained institutional learning.
This commitment to reskilling must cross the corporate threshold; it must extend directly to factory floors, where the vulnerability to displacement is highest and social safety nets are thinnest.
Ultimately, we must recognize the boundaries of this technology. While AI fundamentally excels at pattern scanning, data aggregation, and workflow automation, it cannot replace the human core.
AI is unrivaled at processing colossal data sets, identifying hidden operational patterns, and executing synchronous workflows. It cannot, however, emulate authentic human empathy, decipher subtle cultural nuances, navigate complex interpersonal conflicts, or provide ethical leadership during an organizational crisis.
Bangladeshi HR leaders must deliberately prioritize emotional intelligence, psychological safety, and ethical decision-making. We must build accessible internal pathways for current employees to acquire functional AI competencies, rather than short-sightedly replacing them with technology-native recruits.
Bangladesh finds itself at a unique historical crossroads. Our vast youth demographic represents an enviable macroeconomic asset that few ageing Western or East Asian nations possess. Yet, this demographic dividend is not a guarantee of prosperity; it is a time-sensitive window of opportunity.
To prevent widespread economic disenfranchisement, an integrated coalition of government institutions, academic policy-makers, corporate leaders, and HR strategists must collaborate. We must build a workforce capable of thriving in a hybridized economy, not merely within the air-conditioned corporate suites of Gulshan and Banani, but also across the industrial manufacturing zones of Gazipur, Savar, and Narayanganj.
AI will undoubtedly redefine the mechanics of labour, but its ultimate socio-economic outcomes must remain anchored by human purpose. The future will not belong to the organizations that achieve total, cold automation, but to those that leverage technology to make their workplaces more profoundly, equitably human.
Aninda Ghosh is senior assistant manager of human resources, University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB).
